q: What are primaries?
a: Primaries change the whole picture, or whole brightness ranges of it: lift, gamma, gain, offset, contrast, saturation, white balance. Do them first; fine work on one colour (secondaries: qualifier, windows) comes after.

q: What do the four colour wheels do?
a: Lift moves the darkest tones (set the black level, tint shadows); Gamma the midtones (brighten or darken the middle, tint it); Gain the brightest tones (set the white level, tint highlights); Offset everything evenly (overall brightness or a colour cast). Each wheel has a puck for colour balance and a jog bar for the brightness of its range.

q: Which wheel controls the highlights?

Each wheel has a puck for colour balance and a jog bar for the brightness of its range.

q: What is the jog bar under a wheel?
a: Under each wheel four boxes show the master (Y) and the red, green and blue offsets: drag a box sideways, or click it and type. Under them the ridged jog bar is the master, the brightness of that range: drag it left or right, double-click it to return to 0. Drag the puck toward a colour to add it; double-click the wheel to centre the puck. Each wheel also has a reset (↺) beside its title.

q: What does the Pivot control?
a: In the number strip: Temp (-100 to 100, 0 neutral) goes cool to warm, blue to orange; Tint (-100 to 100) green to magenta; Contrast (0 to 4, 1 neutral) stretches brightness around the Pivot; Pivot (0 to 1, default 0.336, mid grey) is the brightness contrast leaves alone; Saturation (0 to 4, 1 neutral; 0 is black and white).

q: What's the range of the Temperature slider?
a: In the number strip: Temp (-100 to 100, 0 neutral) goes cool to warm, blue to orange; Tint (-100 to 100) green to magenta; Contrast (0 to 4, 1 neutral) stretches brightness around the Pivot; Pivot (0 to 1, default 0.336, mid grey) is the brightness contrast leaves alone; Saturation (0 to 4, 1 neutral; 0 is black and white).

q: How do I reset a single slider in the primaries?
a: Double-click a control's label to reset just that control. The node's Reset returns every control of the node to neutral.

q: How do I clear everything on a node?
a: Double-click a control's label to reset just that control. The node's Reset returns every control of the node to neutral.

q: Do I start with Offset or with Lift and Gain?
a: There's no single right order. Many colourists balance with Offset first, then shape with Lift, Gamma and Gain; others set the black and white points with Lift and Gain first and balance afterwards. Try both on the same shot and keep the one that gets you there faster.

q: How do I neutralise a green tint from fluorescent light?
a: 1. Select the clip and the node to balance (usually the first) and open Primaries. 2. Click the pen icon at the start of the top strip, WB picker; the Program monitor shows a crosshair. 3. Click something that should be grey or white, or drag a box over a larger neutral area (it averages noise and texture); Esc cancels. 4. Temperature and Tint move so that spot is neutral; adjust them by hand afterwards if the scene should feel warmer.

q: What should I click with the white balance picker?

q: What does Auto balance look at?
a: Use Auto balance (the round A before the picker) when there's no obvious neutral in the frame. It averages the near-grey, mid-tone parts of the whole frame, skipping clipped highlights, deep shadows and strongly coloured areas, and balances on that. Each pick or Auto balance is one undo step.

q: When should I use Auto balance instead of the picker?
a: Use Auto balance (the round A before the picker) when there's no obvious neutral in the frame. It averages the near-grey, mid-tone parts of the whole frame, skipping clipped highlights, deep shadows and strongly coloured areas, and balances on that. Each pick or Auto balance is one undo step.

q: What counts as a clipped spot for the WB picker?
a: The picker refuses a spot that is clipped (its colour is lost), too dark (noise decides) or too colourful to be neutral, and says why. Clipped is judged on the clip's own footage before any node: a channel that reached the top of the camera's signal counts as blown out in every sequence, including DaVinci Wide Gamut and HDR ones.

q: Why can't I pick a blown-out window for white balance?

q: Do keyframed Temperature and Tint work with the picker?
a: Yes: when Temperature and Tint are keyframed, a pick or Auto balance sets a keyframe at the playhead.

q: In Premiere I'd use the Lumetri WB Selector. How do I do that in Revolution?
a: On a node: Primaries ▸ WB picker (click or drag over something neutral) or Auto balance (the round A). Both only move this node's Temperature and Tint, so the numbers won't match Resolve's, which may spread the correction differently.

q: and if it's still a bit blue afterwards?
a: The sliders stay adjustable: raise Temperature by hand a little. If the picker hit the ±100 limit the status line says the cast was only partly removed; balance the rest with the Gain or Offset wheel.

q: What's the first node on an X-M5 clip usually doing?
a: 1. Confirm the clip is interpreted as F-Log2. 2. Select it, add a node, open Primaries. 3. Drag the Gain jog bar right until highlights sit where you want, and the Lift jog bar until blacks are black. 4. Raise Contrast in small steps; keep Pivot at 0.336 unless faces get too dark. 5. Raise Saturation until colours look right. 6. Fix a cast with the WB picker or Auto balance, then Temperature / Tint by taste. 7. Check with the Lumetri Scopes, then Bypass to compare.

q: Which commands read and write a grade?
a: `grade.setParam` sets one parameter (`param`, `value`); `grade.params` lists every parameter with its range; `grade.get` returns the whole grade; `grade.toggleAnimation` turns keyframes on for one parameter (the panel has no keyframe button yet and shows the value at the playhead). Values read from a file are clamped to their ranges.

Values read from a file are clamped to their ranges.

q: How does grade.wb.pick take coordinates?

q: In Premiere I'd grade with Lumetri Color. How does that relate to nodes?
a: Lumetri's wheels and sliders are a separate tool that lives in the clip's effect stack. Nodes run before the effect stack, so a node grade and Lumetri can be combined on the same clip.

q: How do I select a colour with the qualifier?
a: 1. Add a node for the secondary, after your balance and exposure nodes. 2. In Primaries open the Qualifier tab. 3. Click Pick, then click the colour in the Program picture (`grade.pickQualifier`); the qualifier switches on around it. 4. Click Add and click another part of the object to widen it. 5. Set View to Selection or Matte to see what's selected, then back to Normal. 6. Refine with Hue centre / width, Saturation and Luminance low / high, Qualifier softness and Matte blur. 7. Invert acts on everything except the selection. 8. Make the correction in the Primaries tab; it lands only inside the matte.

q: What does a qualifier actually build?
a: It builds a matte (white where the node acts, black where it doesn't) from the node's input picture, before this node and before any Lumetri or effects. The node's corrections (wheels, sliders, curves, grain) then apply only inside that matte.

q: What picture does the qualifier pick from?
a: It builds a matte (white where the node acts, black where it doesn't) from the node's input picture, before this node and before any Lumetri or effects. The node's corrections (wheels, sliders, curves, grain) then apply only inside that matte.

q: What's the difference between qualifier softness and matte blur?
a: Qualifier softness sets how gradual the matte's edges are; Matte blur softens a noisy, speckled matte. Edges that chatter on movement need more softness or blur, not a wider range. If the matte still catches other things, limit it with a window on the same node.

q: My matte catches other things too. What now?
a: Qualifier softness sets how gradual the matte's edges are; Matte blur softens a noisy, speckled matte. Edges that chatter on movement need more softness or blur, not a wider range. If the matte still catches other things, limit it with a window on the same node.

q: Which grade parameters drive the qualifier?
a: All are node parameters set with `grade.setParam` (0…1 unless noted): `qual.on`, `qual.hue`, `qual.hueWidth` (1 is every hue), `qual.satLow`, `qual.satHigh`, `qual.lumLow`, `qual.lumHigh`, `qual.soft` (0.001…0.5), `qual.blur` (σ up to 20 pixels), `qual.invert`, and `qual.show` (0 normal, 1 selection, 2 matte).

q: How do I switch the qualifier view from a script?

q: In Resolve I'd use the HSL qualifier. How do I do that in Revolution?
a: Use the node's Qualifier tab: hue / saturation / luminance ranges, softness, matte blur, invert, Selection and Matte views, and Pick / Add on the viewer. Every node can carry its own qualifier and its whole correction is limited by it. Differences from Resolve: no subtract picker, no RGB / luma-only mode (the 3D qualifier is its own key: the 3D switch on the same tab), one softness for every edge, and the View setting is saved with the node and shows in an export.

Correct in Primaries; the change stays inside the window. ✕ deletes a window.

q: Which commands manage windows on a node?
a: Windows are masks: every `masks.*` command takes `node` instead of `effect`: `masks.add` (shape ellipse, rectangle, polygon, bezier or linear), `masks.set`, `masks.select`, `masks.remove`, `masks.moveVertex`, and `masks.list` lists windows with their node. Paths are in the clip's source pixels.

q: In Resolve I'd use Power Windows. How do I do that in Revolution?
a: Use the node's Windows tab: Circle, Rectangle or Linear (polygon and Bézier shapes through the mask commands), Softness, Invert, and up to 16 windows per node combined by mask mode. Differences from Resolve: a circle is a 4-point Bézier ellipse, there's no separate inside / outside softness, and no outside node yet.

q: In Premiere I'd draw a Lumetri mask. How do I do that on a node?
a: Use the node's Windows tab: Circle, Rectangle or Linear (polygon and Bézier shapes through the mask commands), Softness, Invert, and up to 16 windows per node combined by mask mode. Differences from Resolve: a circle is a 4-point Bézier ellipse, there's no separate inside / outside softness, and no outside node yet.

q: How does window tracking work?
a: 1. Put the playhead on a frame where the window sits well on the subject. 2. In the Windows tab click Track forward (▶) or Track backward (◀); `masks.track` runs in the background and keyframes the window each frame. 3. Scrub to check. If it drifts, move the window back on the frame where it went wrong and track again from there; the new keyframes replace the old ones.

q: How do I make a circle window stay on a moving face?
a: 1. Put the playhead on a frame where the window sits well on the subject. 2. In the Windows tab click Track forward (▶) or Track backward (◀); `masks.track` runs in the background and keyframes the window each frame. 3. Scrub to check. If it drifts, move the window back on the frame where it went wrong and track again from there; the new keyframes replace the old ones.

q: Which tracking methods are there for windows?
a: Revolution's point tracker follows features inside the window with a robust fit. Choose Position, Position + Rotation or Position + Scale + Rotation with `masks.set`'s `trackMethod`. It needs detail inside the window to follow.

q: In Resolve I'd use the Tracker on a window. How do I do that in Revolution?
a: In the node's Windows tab press Track forward or backward on the window. It uses Revolution's point tracker; there's no planar / 3D tracker and no separate tracker graph yet.

q: In Premiere I'd track a mask. How do I do that on a grade window?
